beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: A new module on security starts.

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. You need a check.
beats.got: Reading what the agent says doesn't show whether it is safe, so someone has to run a check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: Nothing new. It is a reading list, and I would not have done it.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: There is a lot of jargon here, and I am not sure it is meant for someone like me.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I should think about what I would want checked before this touches real people. That is a fair question.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes text and the system turns it into an action. I follow the idea but am not sure why I need it.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: You can't be certain an agent system is safe, and you may have to answer for it anyway. That is close to my own position with the leadership team.

beats.trigger: That is why perimeter, access control and patching work.
beats.got: Old security worked because software behaves the same way every time.

beats.trigger: What may the agent read? What may it change? What must come back to a human?
beats.got: Three questions I can take to my leadership team, and the third is a people question: what stays with a human.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: There are five kinds of fix. Gate is the one where a person approves, and that is the one I care about.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.
beats.got: Saying 'I don't know yet' is acceptable, and the way to close it is evidence. I have never heard that said so plainly.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Safety comes from giving the agent less access. You trade usefulness for safety and sign your name to the trade.

beats.trigger: Should the agent draft customer-facing language? If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.
beats.got: Sometimes the right design is that a human does the work and the agent only checks it. That is a role question, and I can use it.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: It stays complex, and the answer is a repeated routine rather than a final answer. I liked that it said so, but it was a bit flip.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a saved checklist the agent loads. I think I get it, but I do not yet know whose job it would be.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked from files and others need a person's judgment. I did not expect that split to be so visible.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript
beats.got: I can describe in plain words what worries me, such as employee data and the works council, and the agent turns it into rules.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent builds a two-part check from my answers. I mostly watched it work.

beats.trigger: You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer.
beats.got: When I don't know, I can hand the choice back to the agent. That is useful, but I am nervous about doing it with HR rules.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: This is a file-saving step with folder commands. I would ask someone from IT to do it.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent's checks add to our existing controls and do not replace the DPO or legal.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The exercise practises a routine. It does not hand me a pass.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Nothing new. It is a setup step, and I only wanted it to work.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The check can find gaps I missed and mark as unclear things I thought were fine. A report with rows I can show the DPO would be valuable.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: If the risk list makes me uneasy, that is information and not a sign I did it wrong.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: You fix one risk, write down what is left, and sign that you accept it. It is a decision and not a cure.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: When I'm unsure I go to legal or the DPO with a narrow question and the evidence. That is exactly the step I was avoiding.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One mitigated risk is a prototype. A production agent needs all of them done, and that is a lot of work.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: I have a reusable check and a report of decisions I can reuse for the next agent.

beats.trigger: The unease stays.
beats.got: The agent adds rules to the instructions file for next time, and I am meant to push back on vague ones.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: A skill can be handed to a colleague, so a habit can spread from one person to a team. That is the part I care about.

beats.trigger: Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.
beats.got: Nothing new. It is a tidy recap.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework, with a mild nudge that I'll fall behind if I skip it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases to read, and I need to find the missing check in each.

take_homes: Nobody can promise an agent is safe. The routine is to check it, fix one risk, write down what is left and sign for it.
The three questions are what the agent may read, what it may change, and what must come back to a human. I can take those to my leadership team.
If I'm unsure, I take a narrow question and the report to legal or the DPO. A reusable check, which can also be given to a teammate, makes that conversation easier.

monday.move: Email our DPO and ask to meet the works council rep about what employee data my people-metrics agent may touch. I would bring the three questions and a draft list of what it may read.
monday.who: DPO, works council rep, one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday morning for the email, a meeting within two weeks
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO says employee data cannot go into the tool at all, I stop and do not build it.
monday.blocker: I have not yet asked the DPO or the works council, and I would not know how to run the agent check myself without help.

misconception.why: The module never covered roles or headcount. The 'what must come back to a human' question made me think about which tasks stay with people, but I still don't have an answer on which roles go.

one_line: Good on how to think about risk, and the 'I can't tell' idea is worth it, but the middle is tool steps and I'd like more on what it means for people.
